summary: Documents how BGP-4 satisfied the requirements for advancing a routing protocol to Draft Standard, summarizing its key features and analyzing scaling and performance. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A check-up report showing a routing protocol is healthy and can handle growth.

questions: how much bandwidth does bgp use
subtitle: A report showing BGP-4 meets the bar for Draft Standard, with a look at its bandwidth, memory and scaling.

tldr.problem: A routing protocol must show it works well and scales before it can advance to Draft Standard, and the Internet was growing fast.
tldr.mechanism: The report summarises BGP-4's key features (path attributes, AS-PATH, incremental updates, aggregation) and estimates the bandwidth, CPU and memory it needs.
tldr.outcome: It concludes BGP should have no scaling problems in link bandwidth or CPU while the Internet is stable, and that memory limits come mainly from IP's flat addressing.

today: RFC 1774 is an Informational report with no obsoleting or updating RFC listed. It analyses BGP-4 as specified in RFC 1771 and reflects the Internet of March 1995.

sections.title: Purpose of the Report
sections.content:
The report documents how the requirements for advancing a routing protocol to Draft Standard have been satisfied by the Border Gateway Protocol version 4 (BGP-4). It summarises the key features of BGP and analyses scaling and performance. It calls itself the first of two reports on BGP.

BGP-4 is an inter-autonomous system routing protocol designed for TCP/IP internets. Version 1 was published in RFC 1105, version 2 in RFC 1163 and version 3 in RFC 1267. The protocol itself is specified in RFC 1771.
sections.eli5: Before a method is promoted to a more official level, someone has to show it really works. This report is that proof for BGP.

sections.title: Key Features of BGP-4
sections.content:
BGP runs between multiple autonomous systems (ASes) and assumes routing inside each AS is handled by some other protocol. It imposes no constraints on the underlying topology, and the information it exchanges is enough to build a graph of AS connectivity from which routing loops can be pruned and some policy decisions enforced.

Its key features are path attributes and aggregation of network layer reachability information (NLRI). Attributes are well-known or optional, and optional ones allow experimentation by a group of routers without affecting the rest of the Internet. The AS-PATH attribute lists the autonomous systems traversed so far, which suppresses loops and supports policy. BGP-4 extends it to hold sets as well as lists, so aggregate routes can carry path information from the routes they summarise.

The algorithm is neither pure distance vector nor pure link state. A full AS path lets a router reconstruct much of the topology, like link state, while exchanging only the routes currently in use is like distance vector. After the initial exchange, peers send only changes (incremental updates), which requires reliable transport, so BGP uses TCP.
sections.eli5: Each route carries a list of the neighbourhoods it passed through, so a message can never go round in circles. After the first big exchange, neighbours only share what changed.

sections.title: Bandwidth and CPU Cost
sections.content:
Right after a connection is set up, peers exchange their complete routing information. With N routes, mean AS distance M and A autonomous systems, the worst-case bandwidth is O(N + M * A). The report's table gives, for example, 49,000 bytes for 10,000 NLRI, mean AS distance 15 and 300 ASes, and 86,000 bytes for 20,000 NLRI, 8 and 400, which it marks as the actual size of the Internet when the document was published.

BGP-4 with CIDR introduced the supernet, a power-of-two aggregation of more than one class-based network. In January 1994 a full-routing router had about 19,000 network entries, with growth estimated at over 1000 new networks per month. A sample at the end of November 1994 showed about 21,000 entries instead of the expected 30,000.

When the Internet is stable, BGP uses only KEEPALIVE messages, suggested every 30 seconds and 19 octets long, which the report puts at about 5 bits/sec of bandwidth. When it is unstable, only changes travel in UPDATE messages, with a worst case of O(C * M) for C changes per second. In steady state, cost does not depend on the number of networks. The report says instability mostly comes from ill-behaved routing inside autonomous systems, not from BGP, and that dampening is a local matter.

EGP, by contrast, exchanges complete information periodically, usually every 3 minutes. The report says even BGP's extreme worst case equals EGP's steady state.
sections.eli5: When calm, BGP only sends a tiny 'still here' note every so often. It only shares news when something changes, which saves a lot compared with repeating everything over and over.

sections.title: Memory and Scaling Limits
sections.content:
Worst-case memory is O((N + M * A) * K), where K is the number of BGP peers. On the NSFNET Backbone (N = 2110, A = 59, M = 5), storing AS paths added less than 7 percent to total memory, compared with the earlier EGP requirement of O(N * K).

Since mean AS distance grows very slowly, memory is dominated by the number of networks times the number of peers. The report's table runs from 27,000 for 2,100 networks to 1,040,000 for 100,000 networks.

The report quotes a 1990 review saying BGP does not scale well because of the flat IP address space, since any routing protocol must carry network numbers. CIDR and BGP-4 reduce that limit, but cannot erase history or fix inefficient assignment of future address blocks. It adds that BGP-like protocols could scale much further with hierarchies of autonomous systems and more flexible aggregation.
sections.eli5: Remembering every address takes space, and that is mostly because of how addresses were handed out, not because of BGP. Grouping addresses together helps.

sections.title: Where BGP Applies
sections.content:
BGP enforces policy under the hop-by-hop routing paradigm: an AS advertises to neighbours only routes it uses itself. Policies needing something else, such as source routing, cannot be supported. BGP does not let one AS send traffic to a neighbour intending that it take a different route from the neighbour's own traffic.

The report argues BGP is nearly a necessity, since operational experience showed EGP to be highly inadequate: it imposes topological restrictions and cannot exchange information efficiently, which causes severe routing instability. BGP was kept minimal but extensible. The report is unsure it would suit non-IP internetworks or other routing paradigms. The memo says security issues are not discussed.
sections.eli5: BGP works well for passing traffic along one hop at a time, which is how the Internet worked then. It cannot do things that need a whole route chosen in advance.
